title: Deferred Taxes & Valuation Allowances
description: Work through deferred tax calculations, realizability, and valuation allowance analysis.
html:
Deferred Taxes & Valuation Allowances

Deferred tax accounting reflects the future tax consequences of temporary differences between financial statement carrying amounts and tax bases.

1. Review: DTA vs. DTL

Future Taxable Amount Deferred Tax Liability
Future Deductible Amount Deferred Tax Asset
Taxable Temporary Difference × Enacted Tax Rate = DTL Deductible Temporary Difference × Enacted Tax Rate = DTA

2. Deferred Tax Asset Example

Assume a company recognizes a $100,000 expense for financial reporting purposes this year, but the expense will not become deductible for tax purposes until a future period.

If the enacted future tax rate is 25%:

$100,000 × 25% = $25,000 DTA

The DTA represents a potential future tax benefit.

3. Realizability of Deferred Tax Assets

Recognizing a deferred tax asset does not automatically mean the company expects to realize the entire benefit.

Management must evaluate whether sufficient future taxable income is expected to be available to realize the deferred tax asset.

4. Valuation Allowance

A valuation allowance is recognized when, based on available evidence, it is more likely than not that some portion or all of a deferred tax asset will not be realized.

More Likely Than Not:

This means a likelihood of more than 50%.

Gross DTA − Valuation Allowance = Net DTA Expected to Be Realized
Example

A company has a gross deferred tax asset of $80,000.

Based on available evidence, management determines that $30,000 of the benefit is more likely than not to be unrealized.

Gross DTA $80,000 − Valuation Allowance $30,000 = Net DTA $50,000

5. Evidence About Realizability

Management considers both positive and negative evidence when evaluating whether a deferred tax asset will be realized.

Positive Evidence Supports Future Realization
Negative Evidence Suggests Benefit May Not Be Realized

Negative evidence may include significant cumulative losses in recent years or expectations of future losses.

Positive evidence may include sufficient expected future taxable income or other available sources of taxable income.

6. Changes in the Valuation Allowance

The valuation allowance is reassessed at each reporting date.

If expectations improve, the valuation allowance may decrease.

If realization becomes less likely, the valuation allowance may increase.

CPA Concept:

The valuation allowance does not eliminate the underlying gross DTA. It reduces the amount of the DTA recognized as expected to be realized.

7. Enacted Tax Rates

Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured using enacted tax rates expected to apply when the temporary differences reverse.

Proposed tax rates are not used merely because management expects them to become law.

Enacted Rate Use It
Proposed But Not Enacted Rate Do Not Use It

8. Change in Enacted Tax Rate

If a new tax rate is enacted, existing deferred tax assets and liabilities are remeasured using the newly enacted rate expected to apply when the temporary differences reverse.

Example

A company has a $200,000 taxable temporary difference.

The enacted rate expected when it reverses changes from 25% to 30%.

Old DTL: $200,000 × 25% = $50,000 New DTL: $200,000 × 30% = $60,000 Increase in DTL: $10,000

9. Permanent Differences

Remember that permanent differences do not reverse in future periods.

Therefore, they do not create deferred tax assets or deferred tax liabilities.

CPA Exam Memory Rule

Future Taxable → DTL Future Deductible → DTA DTA May Not Be Realized → Valuation Allowance Measure Deferred Taxes → Enacted Future Rate Permanent Difference → No DTA / DTL

Key Takeaways

  • Future taxable amounts generally create deferred tax liabilities.
  • Future deductible amounts generally create deferred tax assets.
  • A valuation allowance is required when it is more likely than not that some or all of a DTA will not be realized.
  • Gross DTA minus the valuation allowance gives the net amount expected to be realized.
  • Deferred taxes use enacted tax rates expected to apply when differences reverse.
  • Existing deferred tax balances are remeasured when applicable enacted tax rates change.
  • Permanent differences do not create deferred tax balances.

quiz.prompt: A company has a gross deferred tax asset of $120,000. Based on available evidence, management determines that $45,000 of the tax benefit is more likely than not to be unrealized. What net deferred tax asset should the company report?
quiz.explanation: The company records a $45,000 valuation allowance against the $120,000 gross deferred tax asset. Therefore, the net deferred tax asset is $120,000 − $45,000 = $75,000.
